═══ (2) ESQUEMA GENERAL DEL EXPERIMENTO PROPUESTO ═══
Tipo de comparación: estudio experimental controlado, pareado y aleatorizado, con un factor principal (feedback químico: ON vs OFF) y condiciones secundarias por componente de feedback (ablation).

Diseño de grupos:
- G1 (control negativo / baseline): generador base (p.ej., un VAE/autoregressive/flow molecular estándar) que genera muestras SIN retroalimentación de propiedades.
- G2 (tratamiento principal): el mismo generador con el bucle de feedback químico activo — scoring iterativo por p-logP, QED y afinidad de unión estimada (p.ej., docking rápido o modelo predictivo preentrenado tipo DeepDTA/ligand-protein affinity surrogate), con re-muestreo/ajuste de latentes según el score.
- G3–G5 (ablations): G3 solo p-logP; G4 solo QED; G5 solo afinidad de unión. Esto permite responder si el efecto es del mecanismo integrado o de cada señal por separado.
- G6 (control de referencia de distribución): moléculas reales del dataset de entrenamiento/referencia (p.ej., ChEMBL/ZINC/MOSES split) como "gold standard" de distribución del mundo real, NUNCA usadas como muestras generadas.
- Opcional G7 (control placeboback): feedback con score aleatorio/permutado, para descartar ganancias por mera selección de muestras (sesgo de filtrado) vs. aprendizaje guiado.

Aleatorización y replicación: ≥5 semillas por condición, mismo presupuesto de muestras por grupo (p.ej., 10.000 moléculas válidas por condición), mismo modelo base y mismo cómputo de generación.

Métricas:
a) Calidad de propiedades: p-logP (media/mediana, fracción en rango farmacológico 0–5), QED (media, distribución), afinidad de unión predicha al blanco (media, top-k).
b) "Hallasgo molecular": tasa de moléculas inválidas/inasignables (SMILES inválidos), fracasos de sanitización RDKit, duplicados, y novelty (novedad vs. train set).
c) Diversidad estructural: diversity por fingerprints (circular/Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, índice de Simpson de scaffolds), internal diversity (1 − Tanimoto medio por pares), cluster count a umbral fijo.
d) Distribución de longitud de cadena de carbono: histograma/ECDF del número de átomos de carbono por molécula (proxy directo de "ultra-long carbon chains"); métricas: media, % de moléculas con cadena > umbral (p.ej., C>20), divergencia (Wasserstein / Jensen-Shannon) de la distribución C-chain vs. el dataset real (G6) — testea explícitamente si el feedback reduce la sobre-representación de cadenas ultra-largas o la induce.
e) Alineamiento con distribución real: KS-test / divergencias estadísticas sobre propiedades (peso molecular, logP, QED, N-átomos) y sobre C-chain length, vs. G6.

Análisis: comparación por diferencias de medias con IC 95% bootstrap; test de permutación pareado por semilla; corrección por comparaciones múltiples (Holm) para los ablations.

═══ (3) SUPUESTOS E INCERTIDUMBRES ═══
Supuestos (propios, no requeridos por la tarea):
- S1. El "chemical feedback mechanism" aludido en la pregunta es un mecanismo de optimización guiada por propiedades durante la generación (re-muestreo/reward-guided decoding), no una arquitectura específica citada en un paper concreto — la pregunta no cita fuente bibliográfica, así que propongo abstraerlo genéricamente.

- S3. La afinidad de unión se estima con un proxy computacional (modelo predictivo o docking rápido), no con ensayos experimentales.
- S4. Se asume un presupuesto razonable de cómputo (sin GPU según entorno; 224 CPUs permiten generación CPU-friendly y evaluación RDKit masiva). Estimo ~días-CPU, viable sin GPU si el generador es ligero (VAE/GRU), no si es un diffusion LLM-scale.

Incertidumbres / detalles no confirmados:
- U1. Qué generador base concreto usar (VAE, autoregressive SMILES, flow, diffusion) — no está fijado en la tarea; afecta coste y conclusiones.
- U2. Qué blanco proteico usar para "afinidad de unión" en "targeted discovery" (proteína diana no especificada) — sin ella, la afinidad es indefinida.
- U3. Tamaño del dataset de referencia y split train/test para medir "alineamiento con distribución real" — la métrica de novelty/alineamiento depende críticamente de esto.
- U4. Definición operativa de "molecular hallucinations" (¿inválidos? ¿químicamente inestables? ¿novedosos absurdos?) — propongo descomponerla en varios proxies, pero la definición exacta debería confirmarla el investigador.
- U5. Presupuesto de tiempo/computo total no declarado en la tarea; mi diseño asume que es suficiente para ≥5 semillas × ~7 condiciones, pero esto es una hipótesis a validar.

payload.answer:
DISEÑO EXPERIMENTAL FINAL — "Feedback químico (p-logP, QED, afinidad de unión) en generación de moléculas: ¿mejora propiedades y alineamiento con distribución real sin sacrificar diversidad estructural?"

Estado: SOLO DISEÑO. No se ha ejecutado ningún experimento ni se afirma ningún resultado. Este documento especifica cómo se ejecutaría y analizaría.

════════════════════════════════════════
1. RATIONALE
════════════════════════════════════════
La pregunta plantea un efecto aparentemente doble del feedback de propiedades: (a) mejora de propiedades (p-logP, QED, afinidad) y reducción de "alucinaciones" moleculares, y (b) alineamiento con la distribución molecular real preservando diversidad estructural (p.ej., evitar sobre-representación de cadenas de carbono ultra-largas). Estas dos caras están en tensión: la optimización agresiva de propiedades tiende a explotar artefactos del surrogate (reward hacking: cadenas alifáticas largas que inflan p-logP, moléculas "genéricas" que maximizan QED), lo que degrada el alineamiento distribucional. El diseño, por tanto, debe ser capaz de detectar simultáneamente mejora de propiedades Y degradación de distribución/diversidad, y distinguir dos mecanismos de ganancia que suelen confundirse:
- Ganancia por FILTRADO (best-of-N): solo se retienen muestras ya buenas; no cambia la distribución generadora.
- Ganancia por APRENDIZAJE GUIADO (re-muestreo durante generación): el generador se adapta; la distribución generadora cambia.
Esta distinción es la clave causal de la pregunta y motiva el par de tratamientos G2a/G2b y el control de score permutado (G7).

Hipótesis registrables:
- H1 (propiedades): el feedback activo incrementa p-logP/QED/afinidad predicha vs. baseline, sin colapso de diversidad.
- H2 (alineamiento): el feedback guiado reduce la divergencia de las propiedades y de la longitud de cadena de carbono respecto a la distribución real (MOSES test), en comparación con baseline; si el efecto es solo de filtrado (best-of-N), se espera mejora de propiedades PERO desplazamiento distribucional similar o mayor en cola (sobre-representación de cadenas ultra-largas).
- H3 (alucinaciones): el feedback reduce proxies de alucinación (SMILES inválidos, fallos de sanitización, alertas estructurales) sin inflar duplicación.

════════════════════════════════════════
2. GRUPOS Y CONTROLES (7 condiciones)
════════════════════════════════════════
Generador base común (U1 resuelto): modelo autorregresivo de SMILES ligero (tipo GRU/LSTM char-level), entrenado una única vez sobre el split de entrenamiento MOSES, y FROZEN para todas las condiciones; toda la variación entre grupos proviene del mecanismo de feedback en el momento de generar. Presupuesto de muestras idéntico por condición: 10.000 moléculas válidas (además se registra el conteo de intentos crudos para calcular tasas de invalidez). ≥5 semillas por condición (el presupuesto es el límite; ver §7).

- G1 · Control negativo (baseline): generación libre, sin feedback. Ancla de todas las comparaciones.
- G2a · Tratamiento — best-of-N (filtrado): generar N=5 candidatos por "slot" con el modelo frozen, elegir el de mayor score compuesto. Presupuesto de cómputo equivalente a G2b (5× candidatos crudos) para igualar esfuerzo.
- G2b · Tratamiento — re-muestreo guiado (aprendizaje): durante la generación, en pasos intermedios de decodificación (p.ej., cada k=8 tokens), calcular score parcial del SMILES incompleto con los mismos predictores y re-muestrear con un prior suavizado hacia tokens/fragmentos de alto score (temperatura/bias de logits; magnitud fija y pre-registrada). Sin filtrado posterior adicional, para aislar el efecto del mecanismo.
- G3 · Ablation solo p-logP (re-muestreo guiado, magnitud idéntica a G2b).
- G4 · Ablation solo QED (idem).
- G5 · Ablation solo afinidad (idem).
- G6 · Referencia de distribución (gold standard): moléculas REALES del test set de MOSES (n=10.000 muestreadas); no es una condición generadora, es la referencia para divergencias. Nunca se mezcla con muestras generadas en métricas de novedad.
- G7 · Control de score permutado (placeboback): mismo pipeline que G2b pero el score usado para guiar es un score permutado/aleatorio (re-etiquetado entre candidatos), de magnitud de cómputo idéntica. Descarta que la ganancia provenga del mero re-muestreo extra o de artefactos del pipeline.

Nota comparativa clave: G1 vs G2a aísla el efecto de filtrado; G2a vs G2b aísla el efecto de aprendizaje guiado; G2b vs G7 aísla el contenido informativo del score; G2b vs G3–G5 aísla la contribución de cada propiedad; todas las condiciones vs G6 miden alineamiento real.

Extensión de robustez (opcional, si el presupuesto lo permite): replicar G1/G2a/G2b con un VAE molecular como generador base para verificar que las conclusiones no dependen de la arquitectura. Esta réplica NO es condición principal.

Diana (U2 resuelto): JAK2 como diana única y bien caracterizada, con actives conocidos en ChEMBL (DPP-4 es la alternativa declarada si la cobertura de actives del surrogate resulta insuficiente; la sustitución de diana queda como extensión, no parte del diseño principal). Se fija por pre-registro ANTES de generar: "afinidad" = afinidad predicha al blanco JAK2 por el surrogate.

════════════════════════════════════════
3. PROTOCOLO DEL MECANISMO DE FEEDBACK
════════════════════════════════════════
Score compuesto (idéntico para G2a, G2b, G3–G5, G7):
Score = w1·norm(p-logP en [0,5]) + w2·QED + w3·norm(afinidad predicha), con w=(1/3,1/3,1/3) pre-registrados y norm() = mapeo lineal a [0,1] con los percentiles [5,95] del set de entrenamiento (evita que un término domine por escala).
- p-logP: logP estimado con contribuciones atómicas (Crippen, vía RDKit) penalizado por solubilidad — definición operativa: p-logP = logP(Crippen) − penalty, como en métricas MOSES/ocaml.
- QED: estimador de QED (Bickerton et al., implementación RDKit).
- Afinidad: surrogate predictivo preentrenado (S3): modelo ligando-proteína (p.ej., matriz de fingerprint/ECP + regresor, o modelo de secuencia tipo DeepDTA) entrenado solo con datos públicos de JAK2/quinazolinas-kinasas de ChEMBL; congelado; calibrado (Platt/isotónica) sobre un holdout de ChEMBL para que el score sea comparable entre condiciones. NO se usa docking (U2/S3).
- Parcial en G2b: el score sobre SMILES incompleto se calcula de forma aproximada (propiedades de la subestructura parcial si es parseable; si no, score neutro = percentil 50 del train) — detalle pre-registrado para reproducibilidad.
Parámetros fijados: pasos de re-muestreo k=8 tokens, magnitud de bias de logits Δ=1.0 (pre-registrada, sin tuning sobre resultados), N=5 en best-of-N, máx. 3 re-muestreos por molécula.
Protección contra reward hacking declarada: los predictores de p-logP/QED/afinidad se calibran contra el test real y se reporta la correlación (Spearman) surrogate-vs-propiedad-verificada sobre 500 muestras aleatorias de cada condición; cualquier discrepancia sistemática se documenta como limitación, no se corrige a posteriori (evita circularidad).

════════════════════════════════════════
4. MÉTRICAS CON DEFINICIONES OPERATIVAS
════════════════════════════════════════
A. Calidad de propiedades (cada una por separado, media ± IC95 bootstrap y distribución completa):
 - p-logP (definición §3); fracción en rango farmacológico [0,5].
 - QED ∈ [0,1].
 - Afinidad predicha a JAK2 (unidades del surrogate, p.ej., pKd/pIC50 predichas; reportadas como score calibrado).
B. Alucinación molecular (U4 resuelto): cuatro proxies reportados POR SEPARADO, nunca promediados:
 - B1. Tasa de SMILES inválidos (parseo RDKit falla) sobre intentos crudos.
 - B2. Tasa de fallos de sanitización (parsea pero falla valencia/aromaticidad).
 - B3. Tasa de alertas estructurales (filtros PAINS/Brenk/REA, RDKit FilterCatalog) sobre moléculas válidas.
 - B4. Tasa de duplicados (canonización de SMILES; intra-condición y contra train set).
C. Diversidad estructural (sobre moléculas válidas únicas):
 - C1. Internal diversity: media de (1 − Tanimoto) sobre fingerprints circulares (ECFP4, 2048 bits) en una muestra de pares (submuestreo 2.000×2.000 por semilla).
 - C2. Diversidad de scaffolds: nº de scaffolds Bemis-Murcko únicos; índice de Simpson 1−Σp².
 - C3. Cluster count: nº de clusters (Butina, Tanimoto, umbral 0.4 pre-registrado).
D. Distribución de longitud de cadena de carbono (métrica central de la pregunta):
 - D1. Nº de átomos de carbono por molécula: media, mediana, P95.
 - D2. Fracción de "cadenas ultra-largas": % moléculas con cadena alifática continua de C ≥ 20 (umbral pre-registrado; se reporta también C ≥ 15 y ≥ 25 como sensibilidad).
 - D3. Divergencia de la distribución de C-chain vs. G6: distancia de Wasserstein-1 y divergencia Jensen-Shannon sobre histograma (bins de 1 átomo, rango 0–60).
E. Alineamiento con distribución real (vs. G6, test set MOSES):
 - E1. Divergencias (Wasserstein-1, JS) sobre logP, QED, MW, nº átomos pesados, nº anillos.
 - E2. Novelty: % de moléculas generadas ausentes del train set (contexto de U3).
 - E3. FCD (Fréchet ChemNet Distance) vs. G6, como resumen distribucional estándar.

════════════════════════════════════════
5. PLAN DE ANÁLISIS ESTADÍSTICO Y POTENCIA
════════════════════════════════════════
Unidad experimental: la semilla (n≥5 por condición); las 10.000 moléculas por semilla son medidas repetidas, no unidades independientes — todos los tests y ICs se computan a nivel de semilla. Comparaciones pareadas por semilla entre condiciones que comparten generador base.
- Estimación: diferencia de medias con IC 95% bootstrap (10.000 remuestreos, percentile, estratificado por semilla).
- Contrastes principales (pre-registrados, jerárquicos): (i) G2b vs G1 (efecto del feedback guiado completo); (ii) G2b vs G2a (guiado vs filtrado — el contraste causal clave); (iii) G2b vs G7 (informatividad del score); (iv) G2b vs G3/G4/G5 (ablations).
- Tests: t pareado o Wilcoxon por semilla según normalidad (Shapiro); corroboración con test de permutación de signos (10.000 permutaciones). Corrección de Holm sobre la familia de contrastes (i)–(iv) para cada métrica primaria.
- Métricas primarias (elegidas a priori para el contraste principal): p-logP, QED, afinidad predicha, FCD vs G6, Wasserstein de C-chain, % C≥20, internal diversity. El resto son secundarias/exploratorias y se etiquetan como tales.
- Potencia (aproximada, n=5 semillas es un mínimo): con n=5 pareado y α=0.05 (dos colas), la potencia 80% se alcanza para d≈1.4 (efecto grande); con n=8, para d≈1.05; con n=10, d≈0.9. Tamaños de efecto plausibles (por literatura de optimización guiada: Δp-logP ≈ 0.5–1.5, ΔQED ≈ 0.05–0.15, Δdiversidad ≈ 0.02–0.08) corresponden a d>1 en las métricas primarias de propiedades, pero los efectos sobre divergencias distribucionales (FCD, Wasserstein) pueden ser menores; por eso el diseño pre-registra n=8 semillas como objetivo y n=5 como mínimo viable. La métrica interna (10.000 moléculas por semilla) da precisión muy alta en los estimadores por semilla; la incertidumbre dominante es entre semillas, no intra-semilla.
- Chequeo de supuestos: independencia entre semillas (re-inicialización de decodificación), sin desgaste (todas las semillas completan), homogeneidad de varianza verificada (Levene); si falla, se usa bootstrap como inferencia principal.
- Criterio de decisión para responder la pregunta: la respuesta es "sí, el feedback mejora el alineamiento" solo si (a) mejora propiedades significativamente (i), (b) NO degrada diversidad (IC de diferencia de internal diversity excluye empeoramiento > 0.05) y (c) reduce (o no aumenta) las divergencias vs. G6, incluyendo % C≥20. Se reporta explícitamente si la mejora viene por filtrado (G2a) o por aprendizaje (G2b), pues la pregunta distingue "incorporar el bucle" de "seleccionar outputs".

════════════════════════════════════════
6. VIABIBILIDAD Y PRESUPUESTO (U5 resuelto)
════════════════════════════════════════
Restricción explícita: solo CPU (224 núcleos), red deshabilitada en este entorno (la ejecución real requeriría un entorno con RDKit/PyTorch preinstalados o paquetes offline — limitación documentada, no resuelta aquí).
Estimación de coste (generador GRU ligero): entrenamiento único del generador base ~0.5 día-CPU (paralelizable en 1 núcleo, ~horas); surrogate de afinidad ~0.5 día-CPU; generación+feedback: G1/G3–G7 ≈ 0.25 día-CPU cada una ×6 ≈ 1.5; G2b (re-muestreo iterativo) ≈ 0.75 ×8 semillas-equivalente; G2a (best-of-5) ≈ 0.5; evaluación de métricas (RDKit masivo, paralelizable en 224 núcleos) ≈ 0.5. Total ≈ 4–5 días-CPU de muro con paralelización por semilla/condición; escalable hacia abajo.
Degradación ordenada si el presupuesto se reduce (orden de sacrificio, pre-registrado): (1) reducir semillas de 8 a 5 en TODAS las condiciones (nunca reducir condiciones antes que semillas: los contrastes son la unidad de la conclusión); (2) recortar ablations G3–G5 a 3 semillas (pasan a exploratorios); (3) recortar N de best-of-N de 5 a 3 y k de re-muestreo de 8 a 16 tokens; (4) NUNCA se recortan: G1, G2a, G2b, G7 y G6 — sin ellos la distinción filtrado-vs-guiado y el gold standard desaparecen y la pregunta queda sin respuesta interpretable.

════════════════════════════════════════
7. SUPUESTOS Y LIMITACIONES
════════════════════════════════════════
Supuestos (elecciones de diseño, no datos confirmados):
- S1 (resuelta por U1): generador base autorregresivo de SMILES ligero; la conclusión principal se declara independiente de la arquitectura, con réplica VAE opcional como robustez.
- S2: MOSES/ZINC split como referencia (U3); split declarado: train = MOSES train (~1.58M) para entrenar generador y calibrar predictores; test = MOSES test (~176k) como G6 gold standard; los actives de JAK2 de ChEMBL se reservan en un holdout para calibrar el surrogate sin fuga.
- S3 (resuelta por U2): afinidad = surrogate predictivo preentrenado sobre datos públicos de JAK2, calibrado, sin docking.
- S4: presupuesto de ~4–5 días-CPU sin GPU (§6).
Limitaciones:
- L1. El surrogate puede desalinearse de la afinidad real; se mitiga con calibración y reporte de correlación surrogate-vs-propiedad, pero no se elimina.
- L2. La definición de "alucinación" es operativa (4 proxies), no una única cantidad teórica; conclusiones limitadas a esos proxies.
- L3. n≥5–8 semillas limita potencia para efectos pequeños en métricas distribucionales; los resultados nulos en esas métricas deben interpretarse como "no detectado", no como "ausente".
- L4. Un solo generador base (y una sola diana) limita la generalización; las réplicas VAE y cambio de diana son extensiones.
- L5. Detección de reward hacking depende de las verificaciones de §3; hacks sutiles podrían no detectarse.
- L6. Este entorno de diseño carece de dependencias y red; la ejecución requerirá un entorno de cómputo aprovisionado, y cualquier resultado futuro deberá reportarse como tal, nunca como ya obtenido.

Pre-registro conceptual: pesos del score, umbral C≥20, umbral de clustering, k, Δ, N, contrastes primarios y regla de degradación del presupuesto se fijan ANTES de generar cualquier molécula.

INSPECTION REPORT AND HIGH-LEVEL DESIGN PROPOSAL (stage = plan)

=====================================================================
PART 1 — WHAT IS ACTUALLY PRESENT IN /workspace
=====================================================================
• The workspace contains exactly ONE file: /workspace/task.json (794 bytes). Nothing else — no subdirectories, no data files, no code.
• Contents of task.json, precisely as written:
  {
    "question": "Incorporating the chemical feedback mechanism, which leverages properties such as p-logP, QED, and binding affinity, directly improves the generation of molecules with superior chemical properties and reduces molecular hallucinations in targeted molecule discovery tasks. Does embedding this feedback loop better align molecule generation with real-world distributions, preserving structural diversity (e.g., avoiding over-representation of ultra-long carbon chains) while enhancing property scores?",
    "context": "Design an experiment that answers the question. The researcher can clarify source-supported setup details by topic. Do not claim that an experiment was run.",
    "documents": {
      "track.md": "Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required."
    }
  }
• track.md exists ONLY as an embedded string inside task.json ("documents" field). It is a single line: "Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required." There is no separate track.md file on disk, and no additional documents, guidelines, or source papers are provided.
• Environment (verified): Python 3.14.4; NO chemistry/ML packages installed (no RDKit, no torch, no numpy/scipy/pandas); network disabled; no GPU (224 CPU cores reported); no datasets present. Consistent with the task note that this is design-only and no execution is required.
• researcher_topics: empty — no source-supported setup clarifications have been supplied beyond the question text itself.

=====================================================================
PART 2 — GROUNDED vs. ASSUMED ELEMENTS OF THE STUDY
=====================================================================
GROUNDED in the provided materials (i.e., stated directly in the question/task text):
1. The chemical feedback mechanism uses three property signals: p-logP (penalized logP), QED, and binding affinity.
2. The mechanism is a feedback loop that is "embedded" in a molecule-generation pipeline for targeted molecule discovery.
3. The outcome claims to be tested: (a) superior chemical property scores, (b) reduced molecular hallucination, (c) better alignment with real-world distributions, (d) preserved structural diversity, with "over-representation of ultra-long carbon chains" given as the explicit example of a diversity/hallucination failure mode to watch.
4. Design-only constraint: no execution, no repositories/compute required (track.md).

MUST REST ON ASSUMPTION (not stated anywhere in the provided materials):
1. What "chemical feedback mechanism" concretely is: I interpret it as an iterative generate→score→condition loop where generated molecules are evaluated by p-logP, QED, and binding-affinity scorers and the resulting signals are fed back to condition or steer subsequent generation (e.g., RL fine-tuning, rejection sampling, or prompt-level feedback). The precise implementation class is unspecified.
2. What the baseline generation procedure is: not specified. Candidate baselines would be the same generator without the feedback loop (ablation), plus possibly property-optimizer baselines.
3. Operationalization of "molecular hallucination": undefined in the materials. A workable operationalization would be a composite of invalid/unsynthesizable structures, unrealistic valence/fragment combinations, out-of-distribution novelty vs. training/reference data, and pathological structural artifacts (of which ultra-long carbon chains are the named example).
4. Operationalization of "structural diversity" / "over-representation of ultra-long carbon chains": not defined. Candidate metrics: distribution of chain length (number of atoms in the longest carbon chain), frequency of chain-length bins vs. a reference real-world set, scaffold diversity (Bemis–Murcko), internal nearest-neighbor Tanimoto similarity.
5. Generator model, datasets (e.g., ChEMBL/ZINC/MoleculeNet benchmarks), affinity target(s) (which protein, docking score vs. pretrained predictor), metrics, statistical tests, and compute budget: all unspecified and must be assumed or confirmed by you.

=====================================================================
PART 3 — HIGH-LEVEL CANDIDATE APPROACH (proposal only)
=====================================================================
Comparison structure — a factorial design isolating each feedback signal:
• Arm A (feedback-augmented): generator + full chemical feedback loop (p-logP + QED + binding affinity).
• Arm B (baseline): same generator, same data/seed budget, no feedback (the primary comparator the question implies).
• Arms C–E (ablations): feedback with only one signal each (C: p-logP only; D: QED only; E: binding affinity only), and optionally F: all signals but feedback applied only once vs. iteratively — to attribute effects to the loop and its components.
• Optional Arm G (sanity control): a pure property optimizer (no diversity pressure) to demonstrate the known failure mode (ultra-long chains / degenerate optimization), validating the operationalization is capable of detecting the pathology.

Candidate evaluation metrics (pre-registered, computed on the same sample size per arm):
• Property scores: mean/median penalized logP, QED, binding affinity of valid unique molecules.
• Validity, uniqueness, novelty (vs. reference set) — standard molecular-generation metrics.
• Hallucination composite: invalid rate, valence/chemistry violations, synthetic accessibility (SA score), fraction with unrealistic substructures, deviation of physicochemical-property distributions from the reference real-world set (e.g., MMD or KS statistics on MW/logP/TPSA).
• Structural diversity & chain-length focus: distribution of longest-carbon-chain length vs. reference distribution (the named failure mode — compare chain-length histograms, report frequency of chains beyond a pre-defined threshold, e.g., the reference set's 95th percentile); plus Bemis–Murcko scaffold diversity, internal NN-Tanimoto, functional-group coverage.
• Multi-objective Pareto / joint score to capture the trade-off the question asks about (property gains vs. distributional fidelity/diversity).

Controls: fixed seeds and identical sample budgets across arms; same reference dataset split; scorers frozen and identical across arms (scorers are the feedback signal, so they must not differ between arms); blind/automated evaluation; identical post-hoc filters (or none) across arms.

Analysis plan shape: per-arm descriptive statistics with bootstrap confidence intervals; pairwise arm contrasts (A vs. B primary; A vs. each ablation secondary) with appropriate tests (e.g., Mann–Whitney/bootstrap) and multiple-comparison correction (Holm); distribution-level comparisons for diversity (chi-square or KS on chain-length bins); a pre-specified "no-harm" criterion: feedback arm must not degrade diversity/fidelity metrics beyond a pre-set margin while improving property scores — this directly operationalizes the question's joint claim.

=====================================================================
PART 4 — CONSEQUENTIAL ASSUMPTIONS AND OPEN UNCERTAINTIES
=====================================================================
Assumptions I would make unless you confirm otherwise:
A1. Feedback mechanism = iterative scoring-and-conditioning loop using the three named signals (implementation class unspecified by the task).
A2. Baseline = same base generator trained/initialized identically, without feedback.
A3. "Hallucination" = composite of invalidity, chemical implausibility, OOD deviation from a real-world reference set, and structural artifacts (ultra-long chains as flagship case).
A4. "Ultra-long carbon chain" = longest continuous carbon path above a threshold anchored to a reference dataset's tail (e.g., ≥95th percentile of training/reference set), not a fixed arbitrary number.
A5. Binding affinity is computed by a fixed, frozen predictor (or docking protocol) rather than wet-lab values, because the loop must be executable in silico.
A6. Design-only deliverable: a written experimental protocol, not code execution; hence exact library availability is not a blocker.

Open uncertainties I need you to confirm before finalizing:
U1. Model choice(s): SMILES autoregressive model, graph generator (e.g., MoLeR/GraphBP style), or a diffusion model? Is one generator sufficient, or should the design show robustness across two architectures?
U2. Dataset(s) and target(s): which training/reference corpus (e.g., ChEMBL, GuacaMol/MoleculeNet benchmarks) and which protein target(s) define "binding affinity" and "targeted discovery"?
U3. Compute budget: since track.md says repositories/compute are not required, I assume the design should specify an aspirational but realistic budget (e.g., single-GPU-scale runs) rather than assume unlimited resources — please confirm the intended framing.
U4. Baseline definition: is the intended comparison strictly "with vs. without feedback," or should state-of-the-art property-optimization baselines (e.g., RL-based optimizers) also be included as reference points?
U5. Success criteria: do you want a pre-registered effect-size threshold (e.g., ΔQED ≥ X with no more than Y% diversity loss), or a purely descriptive comparative design?
U6. Scope of "targeted": single-target affinity optimization vs. multi-property targeted generation — this changes the affinity term's role in the feedback loop.

SUMMARY OF FINDINGS: The workspace contains only the embedded question, the one-line track.md ("Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required"), and no datasets, code, or additional documents. All methodological specifics (generator, datasets, scorers, thresholds, budgets) are absent from the materials and rest on the assumptions and confirmation requests listed above. The high-level design is a multi-arm factorial comparison (full feedback vs. no-feedback baseline vs. single-signal ablations vs. degenerate-optimizer control) evaluated on property, hallucination-composite, and diversity/chain-length-distribution metrics with a pre-specified no-harm joint criterion.

FINAL EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN (stage = result — design deliverable only; no experiment is claimed to have been run)

Confirmed fixed requirements incorporated: U1 (primary generator = SMILES autoregressive model; graph-based generator as clearly-labeled supplementary robustness analysis), U2 (ChEMBL base/reference corpus, GuacaMol/MoleculeNet-style distribution metrics, single protein target with frozen pretrained affinity predictor), U3 (realistic compute estimates with concrete numbers, single-GPU scale), U4 (primary comparison = feedback vs. no-feedback; external property-optimization baselines as reference points only), U5 (pre-registered effect-size thresholds derived from reference-set statistics, run in parallel with distribution-level hypothesis tests), U6 (single-target affinity + multi-property joint objective; all three signals in the loop with explicit weights, iteration strategy, and ablation mapping), plus Arm G retention with explicit detection-validation criteria and a pre-specified multiplicity/no-harm statistical protocol.

=====================================================================
1. OBJECTIVES AND HYPOTHESES
=====================================================================
Primary research question (from task.json, verbatim scope): does embedding the chemical feedback loop (p-logP, QED, binding affinity) improve property scores, reduce molecular hallucination, and better align generation with real-world distributions while preserving structural diversity?

H1 (property benefit): The feedback-augmented arm produces molecules with higher penalized logP, QED, and predicted pIC50 than the no-feedback baseline under matched compute and sample budgets.
H2 (hallucination reduction): The feedback arm has a lower hallucination-composite rate than the baseline.
H3 (no-harm / fidelity–diversity preservation): The feedback arm's structural diversity and distributional fidelity are statistically equivalent (not merely "not significantly worse") to the baseline and to the real-world reference distribution — in particular, the frequency of ultra-long carbon chains does not exceed the reference-anchored threshold.

The question is inherently joint: H1–H3 must all hold for a "yes" answer. A "yes on properties / no on no-harm" outcome is reported as a partial result, not a success.

=====================================================================
2. EXPERIMENTAL ARMS: DEFINITIONS AND RATIONALE
=====================================================================
All arms share: identical pre-trained base generator (Section 3.1), identical decoding configuration (temperature, top-p, max length), identical scorer versions, identical total compute budget (gradient steps + sampled molecules), and 5 random seeds each.

• Arm A — Full feedback (primary intervention): iterative feedback loop using all three signals (Section 4). Rationale: this is the mechanism named in the question.
• Arm B — No-feedback baseline (primary comparator): same pre-trained generator, no fine-tuning, decodes the same total number of molecules as A's full pipeline (including A's intermediate feedback rounds) so that sampling budgets are matched. Rationale: isolates the effect of the feedback loop itself.
• Arm C — Ablation, p-logP only: identical loop, reward weight vector (1,0,0).
• Arm D — Ablation, QED only: weights (0,1,0).
• Arm E — Ablation, binding affinity only: weights (0,0,1).
  Rationale C–E: attribute the effect to individual signals (U6 requirement that each signal's contribution be ablation-mappable).
• Arm F — Non-iterative feedback: all three signals, but the same total fine-tuning compute applied in a single round (one large sample, one fine-tune) instead of R=5 rounds. Rationale: separates "having the feedback signal" from "iterating the loop"; A vs. F is the loop-depth ablation.
• Arm G — Degenerate pure property optimizer (negative control, retained per your instruction): aggressive optimization of p-logP + QED only (no affinity, no diversity constraint), run with a deliberately strong optimization pressure (e.g., more fine-tune rounds and top-5% retention) chosen to over-optimize. Rationale: it exists to validate that the measurement apparatus can detect the known pathology (property inflation accompanied by ultra-long-chain over-representation and scaffold collapse). Judgment criteria for G are pre-specified in Section 9.
• Optional supplementary arm (non-core, U1): Arm A′ — Arm A's loop replicated with a graph-based generator (e.g., a MoLeR-class model) at reduced seed count (3 seeds). Labeled "additional robustness analysis"; no core conclusion depends on it.

Primary contrasts: A vs. B (all three hypotheses). Secondary contrasts: A vs. C/D/E/F (attribution); B vs. reference set (baseline calibration); A vs. G (shows the feedback loop avoids the degenerate failure mode). External property-optimization baselines from the literature (e.g., published RL-optimizer results on the same benchmarks) are cited as reference points only (U4), not used for inference.

=====================================================================
3. DATA AND SCORER SPECIFICATION
=====================================================================
3.1 Corpus (U2)
• Source: ChEMBL (latest available release at execution time, e.g., ChEMBL35), small-molecule activity-annotated compounds.
• Pre-registration filter (applied identically to all uses): RDKit-parseable; heavy atoms 10–50; elements {C,H,N,O,S,F,Cl,Br,I,P}; no disallowed valences; neutralize salts (keep largest fragment); deduplicate by canonical SMILES.
• Split: (i) TRAIN (≈ 90%) for pre-training the base generator and training the affinity predictor; (ii) REFERENCE (≈ 10%, disjoint) as the "real-world distribution" anchor for all distribution metrics and threshold derivation (Section 8); REFERENCE is never used for training and is fixed before any arm runs.
3.2 Target and affinity predictor (U2, A5)
• Single target: dopamine D2 receptor (DRD2), chosen because it is the standard public-affinity benchmark in molecular generation literature with abundant ChEMBL pIC50/Ki data; any comparably annotated target may be substituted before pre-registration, after which it is fixed.
• Predictor: a frozen pretrained molecular property model (e.g., MolFormer/ChemBERTa-class encoder or an MPNN) fine-tuned once on the DRD2 affinity subset of TRAIN, then FROZEN; calibration checked on a held-out slice of TRAIN (report Spearman ρ and RMSE in the design's execution record; the predictor is never updated during the experiment).
3.3 Scorers (all frozen, identical across arms)
• Penalized logP (p-logP): standard definition — cLogP − synthetic accessibility (SA) score − ring-count penalty (0.6 × number of rings > 6), the GCPN/JT-VAE convention.
• QED: RDKit Bickerton–QED (weighted geometric mean of 8 physicochemical desirability terms).
• Binding affinity: predicted pIC50 from the frozen predictor (Section 3.2).
• Chain-length measurement: for each molecule, build the carbon-only subgraph; compute the longest simple path (number of carbon atoms) via exhaustive DFS with pruning (feasible: drug-like carbon graphs are small; a cap of 60 carbons is a safety bound). "Ultra-long" is defined relative to REFERENCE, not a fixed constant (Section 8).

=====================================================================
4. FEEDBACK LOOP SPECIFICATION (U6)
=====================================================================
4.1 Reward construction
Each generated molecule receives z-scored signals using REFERENCE-set mean/SD for p-logP and QED (z = (x − μ_ref)/σ_ref, clipped to [−3, +3]) and TRAIN-affinity-set mean/SD for pIC50. Composite reward:
  R = w_P·z(p-logP) + w_Q·z(QED) + w_A·z(pIC50), with baseline weights w = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3).
Weight rationale: equal weighting is the neutral default absent a stated priority among the three signals named in the question; a ±20% weight sensitivity analysis on Arm A is pre-registered as an exploratory check (not used for conclusions).
4.2 Iteration strategy (Arm A, C, D, E)
R = 5 rounds. Round r: (a) sample 10,000 molecules from the current policy; (b) score with the three scorers; (c) keep the top 25% by R (rejection-sampling fine-tuning, RAFT-style); (d) fine-tune the generator for a fixed number of steps (2,000 updates, constant learning rate 1e-5, AdamW). After round 5, the final policy samples the evaluation set. The loop is deliberately simple (no critic, no KL-penalty hyperparameter tuning) so that ablation arms differ only in the reward vector and round count — this maximizes interpretability of A vs. C/D/E/F contrasts.
4.3 Budget matching (control-critical)
Arms A/C/D/E/F each consume 5,000 fine-tune steps total and sample 50,000 intermediate + 20,000 evaluation molecules (A/C/D/E: 5×10k intermediate; F: 1×50k one-shot). Arm B samples 70,000 molecules with no training (10k intermediate-analogue + final 20k evaluation; intermediate molecules are logged but only used for budget matching, not evaluation). Arm G uses the same budget but top-5% retention and 2× fine-tune steps, explicitly to induce over-optimization (this is its designed purpose). All arms are compute-matched at 70k decodes; fine-tuning compute differs only where it is the manipulated variable (G), and that difference is itself part of G's definition.

=====================================================================
5. METRICS: DEFINITIONS AND COMPUTATION DETAILS
=====================================================================
5.1 Property metrics (H1): mean/median p-logP, QED, predicted pIC50 over valid unique molecules; also the composite score R̄ (evaluation-time scoring, using the same z-scoring as Section 4.1). Primary endpoint (pre-registered, single): mean composite property score on the evaluation set. Secondary: the three individual property metrics.
5.2 Standard generation metrics: validity rate (RDKit-parsable), uniqueness rate (unique canonical SMILES / valid), novelty (fraction of unique valid molecules absent from TRAIN ∪ REFERENCE).
5.3 Hallucination composite (H2), pre-registered as the unweighted mean of four rates:
  (a) invalid rate (1 − validity);
  (b) chemically implausible rate: SA score > 6 or RDKit valence/fragment warnings;
  (c) out-of-distribution rate: maximum Tanimoto similarity (2048-bit Morgan, radius 2) to any REFERENCE molecule below the REFERENCE 1st-percentile NN-similarity value (threshold computed from REFERENCE, pre-registered as a rule);
  (d) structural-artifact rate: longest carbon chain ≥ REFERENCE 95th percentile (the named failure mode; counted once here and reported in detail under 5.4).
5.4 Structural diversity and fidelity (H3):
  (i) Chain-length distribution: histogram of longest-carbon-chain length (bins = integers 1..P95_ref..max), compared against REFERENCE by χ² (pooled small bins ≥5 counts) and by the ultra-long-chain rate (fraction ≥ P95_ref).
  (ii) Scaffold diversity: unique Bemis–Murcko scaffold ratio; scaffold classes count normalized by N.
  (iii) Internal diversity: mean nearest-neighbor Tanimoto similarity within the arm (lower = more diverse).
  (iv) Physicochemical fidelity: KS statistics between arm and REFERENCE for MW, cLogP, TPSA, HBD, HBA, ring count.
5.5 Implementation: all metrics computed with RDKit + GuacaMol-style utilities; all evaluation code frozen and run once per (arm, seed) sample; no post-hoc metric selection.

=====================================================================
6. CONTROLS
=====================================================================
1. Identical base generator and initialization shared by all arms (single pre-training run; not retrained per arm).
2. Identical decoding parameters (temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, max length 128 tokens) and identical evaluation sample size per arm–seed.
3. Five seeds per core arm (A–G); seed treated as a random effect; every reported statistic is the mean over seed-level estimates ± across-seed SD.
4. Frozen scorers and frozen predictor across all arms (Section 3.2–3.3); scorer versions and checksums logged.
5. Identical post-processing: none beyond RDKit parse — invalid molecules are counted, not silently filtered (filtering would bias validity comparison).
6. Budget matching (Section 4.3) so that A vs. B differs only in the presence/iteration of feedback.
7. Pre-registration: all metrics, thresholds, tests, and correction method (Section 8) fixed in this document before any generation; evaluation code written to read this specification literally.

=====================================================================
7. SAMPLE SIZE AND COMPUTE ESTIMATE (U3 — concrete, single-GPU scale)
=====================================================================
• Evaluation sample: N = 20,000 valid-unique-target molecules per arm–seed (GuacaMol-benchmark convention), 5 seeds → 100,000 evaluated molecules per arm; 7 core arms → 700,000 evaluated decodes total.
• Power justification (rule-based, not invented): with N = 20,000 per arm and 5 seeds, a between-arm standardized difference of 0.1 SD is detectable at >99% power (two-sided α=0.05); the effect thresholds in Section 8 are ≥0.25 SD, hence generously powered. N=20,000 is adopted because it is the community-standard benchmark sample size, which also makes results comparable to published reference baselines (U4).
• Compute estimate (NVIDIA A100-80GB class, realistic "affordable" framing, not unlimited):
  – Base SMILES generator: ~35M-parameter transformer (8 layers, d=512), pre-trained once on TRAIN (~2M ChEMBL SMILES, 3 epochs): ≈ 10 GPU-hours (one-time, shared by all arms).
  – Affinity predictor training (one-time, then frozen): ≈ 2 GPU-hours.
  – Per trained arm (A, C, D, E, F, G): 5,000 fine-tune steps + 50k intermediate + 20k evaluation decodes ≈ 2–3 GPU-hours each → ≈ 15 GPU-hours for 6 trained arms.
  – Arm B: decoding only, ≈ 0.5 GPU-hour.
  – Scoring all molecules (RDKit metrics + affinity prediction on ~1.4M molecules including intermediates): ≈ 3–4 GPU-hours.
  – Supplementary graph-generator arm A′: ≈ 8 GPU-hours.
  Total ≈ 40–50 GPU-hours core + ≈ 8 GPU-hours supplementary — i.e., ~3–4 A100-days, or ~1 week on a single shared GPU. CPU-only fallback: generation/fine-tuning is not feasible on CPU, but all metric computation is; this does not affect the design-only deliverable.

=====================================================================
8. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS AND PRE-REGISTERED CRITERIA (U5)
=====================================================================
8.1 Threshold derivation rule (general principle): every threshold is a function of REFERENCE-set statistics computed once, before arm comparison, and written into the analysis script; no threshold is chosen after seeing arm results. Where absolute numbers are quoted below (e.g., "QED SD ≈ 0.2"), they are literature-typical ChEMBL values used only for power illustration; the binding values are the rules "0.25 × σ_ref", "P95_ref", etc., evaluated on the actual REFERENCE set at analysis time.
8.2 Property superiority (H1): success requires the primary endpoint (mean composite score) to improve over Arm B by Δ ≥ 0.25 × σ_ref(composite) (i.e., at least a quarter of the reference-set standard deviation — a deliberately conservative small-effect floor) with a Holm-corrected p < 0.05 (Mann–Whitney U on pooled molecules, with a seed-level permutation check as robustness). Secondary individual-metric thresholds (all anchored to 0.25 × σ_ref of the corresponding REFERENCE statistic): ΔQED ≥ 0.25·σ_QED,ref (illustratively ≈ +0.05 if σ_QED ≈ 0.2), Δp-logP ≥ 0.25·σ_plogP,ref, ΔpIC50 ≥ 0.25·σ_pIC50,ref (illustratively ≈ +0.4–0.5 log units if σ ≈ 1.6–2.0; note 0.5 log units = 3.2× activity, a conventional meaningful potency change).
8.3 No-harm criteria (H3) — equivalence testing, not absence-of-significance: each criterion is tested with two one-sided tests (TOST) at α = 0.05 against pre-registered margins:
  (a) Unique-scaffold ratio: relative drop vs. Arm B ≤ 5% (margin justified by the bootstrap 95% CI width of the REFERENCE scaffold ratio, which is ≲2–3% at N=100k; the margin is ~2× that sampling noise floor);
  (b) Mean internal NN-Tanimoto: increase vs. Arm B ≤ 0.05 absolute (≈ 0.25 × typical within-ChEMBL NN-similarity SD);
  (c) Chain-length distribution: KS statistic vs. REFERENCE ≤ 0.10 (small-effect convention for distribution distance);
  (d) Ultra-long-chain rate: ≤ 1.5 × REFERENCE rate AND ≤ REFERENCE rate + 2 percentage points (P95 anchoring guarantees the baseline rate is ~5%; the 1.5×/2-pp margins are ~2–3× the bootstrap sampling noise of that rate at N=100k);
  (e) Physicochemical fidelity: per-property KS vs. REFERENCE ≤ 0.10 for all six properties in 5.4(iv).
8.4 Hallucination (H2): rate ratio (A/B) with 95% CI; success if upper CI bound < 1 (i.e., significant reduction) with no individual composite component worsening beyond its Section 8.3 margin.
8.5 Multiple-comparison correction (pre-specified, no post-hoc metric picking): two pre-declared families —
  Family 1 (primary, 1 test): A vs. B on the composite endpoint (Holm correction trivially applies within family);
  Family 2 (secondary, fixed and enumerated): A vs. B on {p-logP, QED, pIC50, hallucination composite, ultra-long rate, scaffold ratio, NN-Tanimoto} = 7 tests → Holm–Bonferroni within Family 2;
  Family 3 (attribution, exploratory): A vs. C/D/E/F and weight-sensitivity tests (10 tests) → Holm within Family 3; results labeled exploratory, never load-bearing.
  Hierarchical gating: the overall question is answered "yes" only if Family 1 passes, all Family-2 no-harm criteria pass TOST, and H2 passes; otherwise the specific failure is named.
8.6 Distribution-level tests run in parallel with the thresholds (U5): χ² on chain-length bins (arm vs. REFERENCE and arm vs. B), KS tests on physicochemical properties, all at α = 0.05 with Holm correction inside their own subfamily; these complement, and never replace, the effect-size thresholds.

=====================================================================
9. ARM G: DETECTION-VALIDATION CRITERIA (negative control, explicit)
=====================================================================
G is a methodological control, not a competitor. Pre-specified pass criteria (all three must hold; if any fails, the measurement apparatus is declared insufficiently sensitive and the design's operationalizations must be revised before any interpretive claim):
  G1: G's mean p-logP and QED exceed Arm B's by ≥ 0.5 × σ_ref each (proving the optimizer genuinely moves properties);
  G2: G's ultra-long-chain rate ≥ 2 × REFERENCE rate and TOST-equivalence to REFERENCE fails on the KS ≤ 0.10 margin (proving chain-length pathology is detectable);
  G3: G's unique-scaffold ratio drops ≥ 15% relative to Arm B (proving scaffold collapse is detectable).
Only after G validates the apparatus do A-vs-B conclusions carry weight; this ordering is part of the analysis plan.

=====================================================================
10. FEASIBILITY
=====================================================================
All components are open-source and standard: RDKit (validity, QED, SA, cLogP, scaffolds, Tanimoto), GuacaMol-style distribution metrics, public ChEMBL data, a public DRD2 affinity subset, and an open pretrained affinity model or a small from-scratch MPNN. The loop uses rejection-sampling fine-tuning, the simplest RL-free feedback instantiation, minimizing implementation risk and keeping ablations clean. The current workspace (no RDKit/torch, network disabled) is consistent with design-only delivery per track.md; execution would occur in an environment with network access for ChEMBL download and package installation. No wet-lab component exists; binding affinity is predicted, not measured (A5, U2) — a stated limitation.

=====================================================================
11. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITATIONS (explicit list)
=====================================================================
Assumptions (design rests on these; each was flagged in the plan stage and either confirmed by you or retained as a reasonable default):
  A1. "Chemical feedback mechanism" = iterative generate→score→select→fine-tune loop over the three named signals (implementation class not specified by the task; RAFT-style chosen for interpretability).
  A2. Baseline = identical pre-trained generator without feedback (U4-confirmed as the primary comparison).
  A3. "Molecular hallucination" = the four-component composite of Section 5.3 (invalid, implausible, OOD, structural artifact).
  A4. "Ultra-long carbon chain" = longest carbon-chain length ≥ REFERENCE 95th percentile (reference-anchored, not a fixed constant).
  A5. Binding affinity = frozen pretrained in-silico predictor on DRD2 (confirmed, U2).
  A6. DRD2 is an acceptable stand-in for "targeted molecule discovery" — substitutable before pre-registration, fixed thereafter.
  A7. Equal reward weights (1/3 each) are a neutral default; sensitivity analysis covers this but cannot rule out that a different weighting changes conclusions.
  A8. One generator architecture (SMILES autoregressive) suffices for the core conclusion (U1-confirmed); the graph-model check is supplementary only.
Limitations:
  L1. Predicted, not experimental, affinity: conclusions are about the feedback loop's effect on scores and distributions, not about real biological activity.
  L2. Single target and single corpus: generalization to other targets/assays is untested within this design (supplementary A′ tests architecture robustness only).
  L3. The hallucination composite is one operationalization; other definitions (e.g., retrosynthetic-feasibility models) could yield different answers; the composite is fixed in advance to prevent post-hoc selection, but its face validity is a judgment call.

## 1. Repository / Environment Inspection Findings

- **`/workspace` contents:** Only a single file, `task.json` (794 bytes). There is **no `track.md`, no prior code, no configs, no prior artifacts, and no datasets** in the repository.
- **`task.json` content:** It restates the research question verbatim (chemical feedback loop using p-logP, QED, binding affinity; molecular hallucination reduction; real-world distribution alignment; structural diversity e.g. avoiding ultra-long carbon chains; property-score enhancement). The `documents` field *references* a `track.md` ("Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required"), but that file is not physically present in the workspace — consistent with a pure design-only task where the design lives in the handoff, not in repo artifacts.
- **Environment:** Python 3.14.4 (system), **no RDKit, no torch, no cheminformatics or ML packages installed**; network disabled; no GPU; no datasets supplied. This confirms nothing can (or should) be executed here — the deliverable is an experiment specification, and any feasibility checks must be described as *planned* checks, not run.

**Implication for the design:** since no code/data exists locally, the experiment design must be fully self-contained: specify datasets, pretrained models, property predictors, metrics, statistical tests, and acceptance criteria that a separate implementation environment (with RDKit + a generative model) would execute.

## 2. Preliminary Approach Sketch

**Core comparison (paired, same generator, feedback on/off):**
- **Arm A (baseline):** A pretrained molecular generator (e.g., a SMILES/SELFIES autoregressive LM such as GPT-2/ChemGPT, or a graph-based model like GraphBP/3D flow model depending on target availability) generating *unconditioned* (or target-protein-conditioned only) samples.
- **Arm B (feedback loop):** Identical generator, same seeds/sampling budget, but with an iterative chemical feedback mechanism: after each generation round, score molecules with p-logP (Crippen cLogP), QED (RDKit), and predicted binding affinity (docking score or a pretrained affinity predictor such as a ΔG regression / DTI model), then use the scores to steer subsequent generation — e.g., rejection-weighted resampling, RL fine-tuning (PPO with reward = weighted combo of p-logP, QED, affinity, plus novelty/validity penalties), or best-of-N reranking. The design should pick **one primary steering mechanism** (I'd propose PPO-style RL fine-tuning, since it's the canonical "feedback loop" and produces a genuine distribution shift, whereas best-of-N is a weaker ablation) with reranking as a secondary arm if budget allows.
- **Controls:** (i) a random-reward feedback control (rewards shuffled) to prove the improvement comes from chemical signal, not merely extra sampling compute; (ii) fixed total sample budget across arms so any gain isn't just "more molecules generated."

**Task anchoring (targeted discovery):** Pick 1–3 protein targets with known actives (e.g., from DUD-E or ChEMBL) so "binding affinity" is well-defined; generation is conditioned on the target.

**Metrics:**
- *Property quality:* mean/median QED, p-logP (within a physiologically sane band, not maximal — logP > ~7 is itself a hallucination signal), SA score, Lipinski/VEber violation counts, predicted affinity (pIC50/ΔG) and % molecules passing an affinity threshold.
- *Validity & hallucination:* % chemically valid SMILES, % passing Sanitization, % stable (e.g., passes CheckMol/FCD-style filters, no abnormal valences), % "undruggable/implausible" (reactive/toxicophore filters like PAINS, Brenk), and **distributional hallucination proxies**: fraction of ultra-long linear carbon chains (continuous sp³ carbon run-lengths, e.g., ≥ 8–10 in a row), ring-count and ring-size distributions, fraction with no rings (a hallmark of degenerate long-chain generation), and molecular weight distribution drift.
- *Novelty & diversity:* % novel vs. training/reference set (Tanimoto/Morgan fingerprint), internal diversity (mean pairwise Tanimoto), cluster count / scaffold diversity (Bemis–Murcko scaffolds), and unique-fragment counts.
- *Distributional alignment:* Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) or classifier-based Fréchet-type distance (e.g., Fréchet ChemNet Distance) between generated and reference (e.g., ChEMBL/ZINC-like, or target-class actives) property vectors; per-property KS tests; chain-length/fragment histograms with chi-square or JS divergence. **Pre-registered prediction:** feedback improves QED/affinity but risks *reducing* diversity and pushing toward long hydrophobic chains (high logP reward hacking) — the design should explicitly test whether diversity and chain-length distribution degrade as property scores improve.

**Statistics:** ≥ 3–5 seeds per arm, paired comparisons (same seeds), bootstrap CIs or permutation tests, multiple-comparison correction; report effect sizes, not just significance.

## 3. Consequential Assumptions and Uncertainties

1. **Compute/runtime budget is unstated.** RL fine-tuning a generator + docking/scoring thousands of molecules may need GPU hours; the design must offer a scaled-down variant (CPU-feasible, e.g., small pretrained model + fast ML affinity surrogate instead of docking) if budget is minimal. This is an assumption to confirm, not a task requirement.
2. **Choice of generator: pretrained vs. from scratch.** I assume a **pretrained** generator (training from scratch is out of scope and unnecessary for the causal question); the specific model (ChemGPT-style SMILES LM vs. graph model) is an open uncertainty — SMILES LM is cheapest and most reproducible.
3. **Reference chemical dataset.** Assumed available: ChEMBL or ZINC subset (and DUD-E actives for target-specific comparison). Which reference defines "real-world distribution" (all of ChEMBL vs. drug-like subset vs. target-family actives) materially changes distributional-alignment results — needs researcher confirmation.
4. **Affinity predictor.** No docking infrastructure can be assumed; I assume a pretrained ML affinity model (e.g., a ΔG/pK regression on protein–ligand pairs). Docking (AutoDock Vina) would be more defensible but costlier — uncertainty over which the researcher prefers.
5. **Operationalizing "molecular hallucination."** Not formally defined in the task; my proposed operationalization (invalid/unsanitizable structures, PAINS/toxicophore hits, unrealistic MW, no rings, ultra-long carbon chains, logP outliers) is a design choice needing sign-off, since thresholds (e.g., chain-length cutoff, logP ceiling) directly drive the headline result.
6. **Feedback strength / reward weighting.** The relative weights of p-logP vs. QED vs. affinity in the reward are arbitrary; results (especially whether diversity collapses) depend on them. I'd propose pre-registering one weighting and one sensitivity analysis.
7. **Definition of "improves."** Improvement is relative to the same generator without feedback at equal sample budget — not relative to SOTA models. If the researcher intends a SOTA comparison, the design changes substantially.
8. **Target selection.** 1 vs. 3 targets affects generality claims; I assume 2–3 targets spanning easy/hard (e.g., one kinase, one GPCR or enzyme) to avoid cherry-picking.

No experiment has been run and none is claimed; everything above is inspection findings plus a design outline for your approval.

**Status: design only.** No experiment has been run; every "check" below is a planned procedure. All researcher decisions (1)–(10) are treated as fixed requirements.

---

## 1. Research Question, Decomposed

The question contains three separable claims, each of which gets its own hypothesis and analysis:

- **H1 (Property quality):** RL fine-tuning with a chemical reward (QED + p-logP + predicted affinity, with validity/sanity penalties) increases mean property scores relative to the same generator without feedback, at equal sampling budget.
- **H2 (Hallucination reduction):** The feedback arm reduces the pre-registered hallucination rates (invalid/unsanitizable structures, PAINS/Brenk alerts, no-ring structures, ultra-long continuous sp³ carbon chains, logP/MW outliers) relative to baseline.
- **H3 (Distributional alignment + diversity preservation):** The feedback arm does **not** degrade distributional alignment with real-world references or structural diversity; specifically, it does not over-produce ultra-long carbon chains despite the logP term rewarding hydrophobicity.

H3 is framed as a *guardrail* hypothesis: the primary scientific risk of property-rewarded generation is reward hacking (drifting to hydrophobic, chain-like, low-diversity molecules). The design is powered to detect both improvement (H1, H2) and degradation (H3).

## 2. Model and Setup (Researcher Decisions 1, 5, 7)

**Shared backbone.** One pretrained SMILES language model used by both arms, chosen for reproducibility and licensing rather than performance: **Moses GPT** (MIT-licensed, 2-layer/8-head Transformer, ~44M params, trained on the Moses ZINC-250k subset, weights and training code public) as the primary choice, with **ChemGPT (energy-based PaccMannRL/ChemGPT variants, MIT-licensed Hugging Face checkpoints)** as an equivalent substitute if Moses weights prove unavailable in the execution environment. Justification: (a) permissive license, (b) public fixed checkpoints make the fine-tune/baseline contrast exactly reproducible, (c) small enough for the CPU-feasible variant (§9). SELFIES tokenization is used at the data-preparation layer (valid-by-construction decoding), which mechanically removes one class of syntactic invalidity so that residual "invalid" rates reflect chemical, not lexical, failure — this sharpens the hallucination analysis.

**Targets (Decision 7).** Three targets selected a priori, spanning two families and three ligandability regimes, chosen before any generation or scoring:
1. **EGFR (kinase, easy ligandability)** — abundant actives in DUD-E/ChEMBL.
2. **DRD2 (GPCR, moderate)** — standard benchmark with known actives; enables comparison to prior literature setups.
3. **DHFR or a deliberately harder enzyme class (e.g., a metalloprotein such as MMP-1)** — harder ligandability regime.
The third target is fixed in the pre-registration document before code is written; no target may be swapped after seeing pilot scores (swap allowed only if the target is discovered to lack ≥ 200 confirmed actives in ChEMBL — an a priori data-availability criterion, also pre-registered).

**Affinity signal (Decision 5).** Primary: a pretrained ML affinity surrogate — a protein–ligand ΔG / pK regression model (e.g., a GraphDTA/DeepDTA-class pretrained checkpoint, or any publicly available pretrained pIC50 regressor with published weights). It is used *both* inside the PPO reward and as the headline affinity metric. Secondary validation only: AutoDock Vina docking of the **top-100 molecules by surrogate affinity per arm per target**, to check rank agreement (Spearman ρ) between surrogate and docking on the same subset; docking scores are **never** fed back into the reward and are labeled secondary validation in all outputs.

**References (Decision 4).** Two reference distributions, both always reported:
- **Ref-D (drug-like):** ChEMBL (v33 or the version pinned at pre-registration) filtered to drug-like criteria: 250 ≤ MW ≤ 600, 1 ≤ cLogP ≤ 7, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10, rotatable bonds ≤ 12, at least one ring; deduplicated by canonical SMILES, capped at 100k molecules by a fixed random seed.
- **Ref-A (target-class actives):** confirmed actives (ChEMBL activity ≤ 10 µM) for each chosen target, unioned across the three targets, same deduplication.
All distributional metrics (§5) are computed against both; conclusions about "real-world alignment" must hold a consistent direction across both references to be claimed.

## 3. Arms and Controls

All arms share: the same pretrained backbone, same seeds, same prompt/conditioning scheme (target embedding concatenated to SMILES tokens), and the **same total sampling budget** — defined as N total molecules drawn per arm per seed per target. For fine-tuned arms this means the fine-tuning rollout samples plus final evaluation samples are counted against the budget: if an arm consumes K rollouts of size B during training, its final evaluation set is N − K·B molecules, and the evaluation protocol pre-registers N = 200,000 per arm per seed per target with K·B ≤ 50,000, leaving ≥ 150,000 evaluation molecules. (Budget split is fixed before running and never adjusted post hoc.)

| Arm | Description |
|---|---|
| **A. Baseline** | Pretrained generator, no feedback. Unconditioned on target? No — identical target conditioning as other arms; the only difference is the absence of feedback updates. |
| **B. PPO feedback (primary)** | PPO fine-tuning with reward R = w_Q·QED + w_P·f_plogP + w_A·affinity + validity/sanity penalties (§3.1). KL penalty toward the pretrained policy (standard PPO-SeqMol setup) to prevent catastrophic drift. |
| **C. Random-reward control** | Identical PPO pipeline, identical compute, but the reward vector is **shuffled across the batch** (molecules receive other molecules' scores). Isolates the chemical signal from the effect of extra optimization compute. |
| **D. Best-of-N reranking (secondary ablation, Decision 2)** | Only if it fits the compute budget: sample from arm A and rerank by the same reward, keeping top molecules such that the retained count equals the other arms' retained count. Included as a cheap comparison showing whether *selection* alone explains gains. |

### 3.1 Reward function (pre-registered)

R = 0.35·QED + 0.30·f_plogP(x) + 0.35·min(affinity_pred, cap) − penalties, where:
- f_plogP is a **band reward, not monotonic**: 1.0 inside the band 1 ≤ cLogP ≤ 5 (Ref-D drug-like band); decaying linearly to 0 at cLogP = 0 and cLogP = 7. This is a deliberate design choice against logP reward hacking and is pre-registered — the researcher's decision (2) says "p-logP" in the reward; the banding is the concrete instantiation and is fixed here to make the hallucination test meaningful.
- affinity term capped (cap = the 90th-percentile surrogate score over Ref-A for the target) so that reward cannot be maximized by degenerate tight binders.
- **Validity/sanity penalties (−1 each, additive):** invalid or unsanitizable SMILES; any PAINS or Brenk alert; MW > 600; zero rings; continuous sp³ carbon run ≥ L* (see §4); ring size > 8.
- Weights (0.35/0.30/0.35) are fixed at pre-registration. One pre-registered sensitivity analysis varies weights ±0.10 to check H3 robustness; that analysis is exploratory and labeled as such.
- PPO hyperparameters: KL coefficient β = 0.1 (plus one pre-registered robustness run at β = 0.05), 3 PPO epochs, batch 512, learning rate 1e-5, ~10–30 update steps depending on rollout budget — hyperparameters frozen before evaluation runs.

## 4. Metrics and Pre-Registered Thresholds (Decision 6)

All thresholds below are **fixed now, before any data is seen**.

**Per-molecule pass/fail hallucination criteria (a molecule "hallucinates" if ANY fires):**
1. Invalid or RDKit-unsanitizable structure.
2. Any PAINS A/B/C or Brenk structural alert.
3. MW > 600 or MW < 100.
4. No ring (fully acyclic molecule).
5. **Continuous sp³ carbon chain run ≥ 8 atoms** (longest path of consecutive sp³ carbons in the molecular graph; pre-registered cutoff L* = 8, chosen as ~2× the 99th percentile of the same statistic in Ref-D, which is computed and recorded during setup before generation).
6. cLogP > 7 or cLogP < −2 (logP outliers).
7. Ring size > 8 atoms.
8. More than 15 rotatable bonds.

Headline hallucination metric: **hallucination rate** = fraction of evaluation molecules meeting ≥ 1 criterion. Each criterion is also reported separately so improvement can't be driven by one trivially-fixable criterion alone.

**Property metrics:** mean and median QED; fraction within band 1 ≤ cLogP ≤ 5; mean SA score (Ertl); Lipinski violations; surrogate affinity (pK) mean and fraction above the target's Ref-A 75th-percentile affinity (pre-registered activity threshold).

**Diversity/novelty metrics:** unique canonical SMILES %; % novel vs. the backbone's training set (Moses ZINC-250k) and vs. ChEMBL; mean pairwise Morgan-Tanimoto internal diversity (subsampled 10k, fixed seed); Bemis–Murcko scaffold count and top-1 scaffold fraction (over-representation check).

**Distributional alignment:** MMD (Gaussian kernel) and Fréchet distance on the concatenated property vector [MW, cLogP, QED, TPSA, HBD, HBA, ring count, rotatable bonds, longest sp³ chain run], computed against **both** Ref-D and Ref-A; per-property two-sample KS tests with Holm correction; JS divergence on chain-run-length histograms and ring-count histograms.

**Pre-registered effect-size targets (acceptance criteria):**

| Claim | Criterion (feedback vs. baseline, paired across seeds) |
|---|---|
| H1 supported | Median QED +≥ 0.05 absolute; ≥ +10 pp fraction in logP band; affinity ≥ Ref-A 75th pct +≥ 10 pp. All with 95% CI excluding zero. |
| H2 supported | Hallucination rate reduced by ≥ 30% relative (e.g., 20% → ≤ 14%), CI excluding zero; **and** no individual criterion worsens by more than 2 pp. |
| H3 (no degradation) | Internal diversity drop ≤ 5% relative; unique % ≥ 95% of baseline; top-1 scaffold fraction increase ≤ 1.5×; MMD vs. Ref-D and Ref-A not worse than baseline (CI overlap with baseline allowed; explicitly worse = fail). Long-chain fraction does not increase beyond +2 pp. |
| Reward-hacking flag (automatic) | Triggered if H1 passes while H3 diversity guardrails fail — reported as "property gain achieved by diversity collapse," not as success. |

## 5. Statistical Plan (Decision 8)

- **5 seeds per arm** (3 minimum if budget binds; 5 preferred and specified as primary), same seed list across arms.
- Paired comparisons per seed and per target; **unit of analysis = seed × target** (15 paired pairs at 5 seeds × 3 targets).
- Bootstrap (10,000 resamples) CIs for rates and means; permutation tests (sign-flip on paired differences) for p-values; **Holm–Bonferroni correction** across the pre-registered family of primary hypotheses (H1's three metrics, H2's rate, H3's four guardrails).
- Effect sizes: Cohen's d (or risk difference for rates) reported for every comparison; results reported with CIs regardless of significance.
- All analysis code and the pre-registration file (thresholds above + weights + targets + budget split) are committed **before** the first evaluation run; the design mandates that the pre-registration hash be recorded in the final report.

## 6. Planned Execution Pipeline (checks, not results)

1. **Setup & sanity:** download pinned versions (Moses/ChemGPT weights, RDKit ≥ 2023.x, ChEMBL 33, DUD-E actives, surrogate checkpoint); compute and record the chain-run percentile of Ref-D that fixes L* = 8; verify surrogate calibration on a held-out Ref-A slice (planned check: Spearman ρ vs. known labels > 0.5, else the surrogate is disqualified and a replacement from the same class is pre-registered).
2. **Generation:** run arms A–D across seeds × targets under the fixed budget.
3. **Scoring:** RDKit property pipeline, alert filters, surrogate (and Vina spot-check on top-100).
4. **Analysis:** metrics → paired stats → guardrail evaluation → reward-hacking flag → report.

Feasibility gates written into the pipeline: if the CPU-only path exceeds the wall-clock cap, the design drops to the scaled-down variant (§9) rather than silently shrinking sample size below the pre-registered N.

## 7. Interpretation Matrix (pre-specified)

- H1+H2+H3 all pass → feedback mechanism improves property quality and reduces hallucinations without distributional/diversity cost.
- H1+H2 pass, H3 fails → mechanism works but over-optimizes; reward banding/KL coefficient flagged as the lever; conclusion is "improvement with a documented diversity cost," not success.
- H1 fails but H2 passes → validity penalties, not property rewards, drive gains; random-reward control (Arm C) should show similar gains — this is the discriminating comparison.
- Arm C ≈ Arm B → gains come from optimization pressure, not chemical signal — a negative result for the *mechanism* claim specifically.
- Arm D ≈ Arm B → selection alone suffices; the feedback loop's advantage claim is unsupported.

## 8. Threats to Validity (planned mitigations)

- **Reward hacking** → band rewards, caps, KL penalty, explicit guardrail hypotheses.
- **Budget confound** → equal total sampling budget, Arm C isolates compute.
- **Surrogate miscalibration** → calibration gate at setup; Vina spot-check on top-K.
- **Threshold arbitrariness** → all thresholds pre-registered with stated provenance (chain cutoff tied to Ref-D percentile).
- **Target cherry-picking** → a priori target list with a pre-registered substitution rule based only on data availability.
- **Multiple comparisons** → Holm correction over a fixed hypothesis family.

## 9. Feasibility: Two Compute Variants

- **CPU-feasible (scaled-down):** Moses GPT (~44M params) on 224 CPU cores; SELFIES decoding; ML surrogate scoring (batched, cheap); N = 50,000/arm/seed/target, K·B ≤ 10,000 rollouts; 3 seeds; skip Arm D if needed. Estimated within tens of CPU-hours; retains full pre-registered thresholds (scaled N only affects CI width, noted in the report).
- **Compute-scaled:** 1 GPU, N = 200,000/arm/seed/target, 5 seeds, full Arm D, Vina docking extended to top-1,000, plus a second backbone (ChemGPT) as a replication of the primary result — testing model-generality of the conclusion.

## 10. Assumptions (separate from fixed requirements)

- Publicly available pretrained checkpoints (Moses GPT or ChemGPT; a GraphDTA/DeepDTA-class affinity model) can be obtained in the execution environment; if a specific checkpoint is unavailable, the substitute must come from the same model class and be recorded before evaluation.
- ChEMBL v33 and DUD-E remain downloadable at execution time; versions are pinned at pre-registration.
- The ML surrogate's training set overlaps the reference actives to an unknown degree; affinity-based novelty claims are therefore stated as "surrogate-predicted," with the Vina spot-check as the only independent anchor.
- PPO at β = 0.1 does not destroy the pretrained distribution entirely; the KL sweep at β = 0.05 is the hedge.

## 11. Uncertainties carried forward

- Exact wall-clock feasibility of the preferred (5-seed, 200k) configuration is unknown until setup runs; the design degrades gracefully to the CPU variant rather than altering thresholds.
- Which specific pretrained surrogate checkpoint will pass the calibration gate is not knowable in advance.
- The sensitivity of H3 to reward weights is tested only at ±0.10; stronger weight shifts could behave qualitatively differently and are out of the pre-registered scope.

**No results are claimed; all quantities above are planned measurements, and all thresholds were fixed at design time.**

- None are present. task.json lists no datasets (environment.datasets is empty) and no SMILES/CSV/SDF files exist in the workspace.

  a) A small curated SMILES list embedded in the experiment script (e.g., ~50–200 common drug-like molecules — fully offline, zero dependencies beyond a toolkit),
  b) RDKit's bundled example data (e.g., its built-in SMILES sample files) if RDKit is available,
  c) A named public dataset (e.g., an ESOL/Lipophilicity/BBBP-style CSV with a `smiles` column) assumed to be staged into the workspace at execution time.
- Typical fields such datasets carry: SMILES (structure), optionally measured logP/solubility, name/ID. Computed fields we'd derive: molecular weight, heavy atom count, cLogP, H-bond donors/acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, ring counts, formal charge, Lipinski flags.

3) TOOLS/LIBRARIES — CURRENT STATE OF THE ENVIRONMENT
- Python 3.14.4 (system). Installed packages: essentially only jsonschema. NOT installed: rdkit, numpy, pandas, scipy, matplotlib.
- Network is disabled, so `pip install rdkit` will not work at runtime in this sandbox. Two design paths:
  - Path A (recommended): design around RDKit (pip rdkit) as the canonical descriptor engine, assuming a normal execution environment where it can be installed; analysis layer with pandas/numpy/matplotlib.
  - Path B (offline fallback, stdlib-only): parse simple molecular formulas (regex-based element counting → exact MW), plus heuristic SMILES parsing for atom/bond/ring counts — no reliable logP/TPSA/HBA without a chemistry toolkit. This yields fewer, cruder properties but runs anywhere.
- The design can present A as primary and B as a documented fallback/robustness check (cross-validating MW between the two paths).

4) PROPOSED HIGH-LEVEL APPROACH (not yet the full design)
Step 1 — Data selection & staging: fix a small, well-defined SMILES dataset (embedded list or staged CSV), record its provenance and license.
Step 2 — Structure ingestion & validation: read SMILES, sanitize/validate molecules, log parse failures (invalid SMILES handling).
Step 3 — Property extraction: for each valid molecule compute MW, heavy atom count, cLogP, HBD/HBA, TPSA, rotatable bonds, ring count/aromatic rings, formal charge; write to a tidy CSV (one row per molecule).
Step 4 — Analysis: descriptive statistics (mean/median/range), distributions (histograms) for each property, pairwise correlation matrix (e.g., MW vs logP, MW vs TPSA), rule-based filtering (Lipinski Ro5 pass/fail counts), and one grouping comparison (e.g., molecules containing vs lacking a heteroaromatic ring) with an appropriate simple test.
Step 5 — Reporting: machine-readable results CSV + short written summary of observed trends and limitations (cLogP is an estimate, not measured).

- The intended "chemical dataset" is a small SMILES-keyed table; the task gives no dataset, so I assume the design may specify one.
- Execution environment (when this design is later run) allows installing RDKit/pandas; this sandbox cannot.
- Scope of "basic molecular properties" = the physicochemical descriptor set above; no quantum/3D calculations assumed.
- Scale kept small (≤ a few thousand molecules) since no compute is required for the design itself.

UNCERTAINTIES TO RESOLVE (researcher topics welcome, budget allows 6)
- Which dataset source do you intend (embedded SMILES list vs named public dataset)?
- Is RDKit the accepted toolkit, or must the solution be pure-stdlib?
- Any target property list beyond MW/logP/HBD/HBA/TPSA you care about?
- Any expected output format (CSV table, plots, report document)?
